pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Identify the different stages of electricity transmission.
- Draw a flow chart to show the stages of electricity transmission from the point of generation to the point of consumption.

pages.title: What is Electricity Transmission?
pages.body: Electricity transmission is the process by which electrical energy travels from the power station where it is generated to the homes, schools and industries where it is finally used. Generation, step up transformation, transmission, step down transformation, and distribution and consumption are the five main stages of this journey.

questions.q: Electricity transmission is best described as
o: The generation of electricity only
The journey of electricity from generation to consumption
The use of electricity in homes only
The use of solar panels only
questions.e: Generation, step up transformation, transmission, step down transformation, and distribution and consumption are the five main stages of this journey.

pages.title: The Stages of Electricity Transmission
pages.body:
Each stage in electricity transmission plays a distinct role in making sure electricity is produced efficiently, carried safely over long distances, and delivered to consumers at a voltage that is safe for everyday use, as summarised in the table below.

| **STAGE** | **WHAT HAPPENS** | **WHY IT MATTERS** |
|---|---|---|
| **Generation** | Electricity is produced at a power station, for example using hydroelectric, thermal or solar power | This is the original source of the electricity supplied to the grid |
| **Step up transformation** | A step up transformer increases the voltage of the electricity before it travels | Higher voltage allows electricity to travel long distances with less energy lost as heat |
| **Transmission** | Electricity travels through transmission lines strung between tall pylons | This carries electricity from the power station to towns and cities, often far away |
| **Step down transformation** | A step down transformer reduces the voltage to a safer level | Lower voltage is needed before electricity can be used safely in homes and small businesses |
| **Distribution and consumption** | Electricity flows through local distribution lines into homes, schools and industries | This is the final stage where electricity is actually used to power lights and appliances |

pages.title: Why Voltage is Changed During Transmission
pages.body: Raising the voltage before transmission and lowering it again before consumption is necessary mainly to reduce energy losses and to keep electricity safe for everyday use. When electricity travels at a high voltage, less energy is lost as heat along the transmission lines compared to transmitting the same power at a lower voltage. However, such high voltages would be extremely dangerous inside a home, which is why step down transformers reduce the voltage to a safer level before it reaches consumers.

lessons.title: Voltages and Organisations in the Supply of Electricity in Ghana

pages.title: Voltages and Organisations in the Supply of Electricity in Ghana
pages.body:
| **STAGE** | **WHAT HAPPENS** | **TYPICAL VOLTAGE IN GHANA** | **ORGANISATION** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Generation** | Generators at power stations produce electricity | About 11 000 to 15 000 volts | Volta River Authority, Bui Power Authority and independent power producers |
| **Step up** | A step up transformer raises the voltage for long distance travel | 161 000 volts, and 330 000 volts on some lines | Ghana Grid Company |
| **Transmission** | High voltage lines on tall steel pylons carry the electricity across the country | 161 000 or 330 000 volts | Ghana Grid Company |
| **Step down** | Transformers at substations lower the voltage in stages | 33 000 volts and then 11 000 volts | Electricity Company of Ghana in the south and Northern Electricity Distribution Company in the north |
| **Distribution** | Transformers on poles near houses lower the voltage for use | About 230 volts for homes and schools | Electricity Company of Ghana and Northern Electricity Distribution Company |

Electricity is sent at a very high voltage because, for the same amount of power, a higher voltage means a smaller current in the cables. A smaller current heats the cables less, so less energy is lost as heat on the long journey from the power station.

- Never fly kites, climb pylons or build under high voltage lines.

- Never touch a fallen power line. Report it to the electricity company at once.

- Keep away from transformers and substations.

pages.title: Look at the picture
pages.body:
[[img:ie27b85732|Fig 6.1  Stages of electricity transmission, from generation to consumption]]

Notice how the voltage of the electricity changes twice during its journey. It is increased shortly after generation to make long distance transmission more efficient, and then decreased again before it reaches homes and businesses, where high voltage would be extremely dangerous.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

In Ghana, the Volta River Authority and the Electricity Company of Ghana play key roles in generating and distributing electricity respectively, while the Ghana Grid Company manages the high voltage transmission network that connects power stations to different parts of the country. Understanding the stages of electricity transmission helps explain why a fault at any single stage, such as damage to a transmission line during a storm, can lead to power outages in areas far from the actual power station.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Research information about capacitors in electronic circuits and explain their functions when connected with direct current (DC).
- Describe the charging and discharging actions of a capacitor, and explain the role of LEDs, diodes and resistors in an electronic circuit.

pages.title: What is a Capacitor?
pages.body: A capacitor is an electronic component made of two conducting plates separated by a thin insulating layer, used to store electrical charge temporarily in a circuit. When connected to a direct current (DC) source, such as a battery, a capacitor stores charge on its plates. Later, when the battery is disconnected or the circuit changes, the capacitor can release, or discharge, this stored charge back into the circuit.

pages.title: Charging and Discharging a Capacitor
pages.body:
Charging and discharging are the two key actions that describe how a capacitor behaves in a DC circuit.

- During charging, a capacitor is connected to a DC source, such as a battery. Current flows into the capacitor, building up electrical charge on its plates, until the capacitor is fully charged and no further current flows.

- During discharging, a charged capacitor is connected into a circuit without the battery, such as one containing a bulb. The stored charge flows out of the capacitor and through the circuit, for example lighting the bulb briefly, until the capacitor is fully discharged.

pages.title: The Role of LEDs, Diodes and Resistors
pages.body:
Capacitors, LEDs, diodes and resistors are four common electronic components that are often found working together in the same circuit, and each plays a distinct role, as summarised in the table below.

| **COMPONENT** | **FUNCTION IN A CIRCUIT** | **EVERYDAY EXAMPLE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Capacitor** | Stores electrical charge temporarily and releases it when needed | Camera flash units store charge in a capacitor before releasing it quickly |
| **LED (light emitting diode)** | Converts electrical energy into light energy, and allows current to flow in only one direction | Indicator lights on phones, radios and remote controls |
| **Diode** | Allows electric current to flow in only one direction, blocking it in the reverse direction | Protecting circuits from a battery being connected the wrong way round |
| **Resistor** | Controls or limits the amount of current flowing in a circuit | Protecting an LED from receiving too much current and burning out |

In many practical circuits, a resistor is deliberately placed in series with an LED to prevent too much current from flowing through it, since excess current can quickly damage or burn out an LED. Similarly, a diode is sometimes added to a circuit to protect a capacitor or other components from being damaged if the current is accidentally connected in the wrong direction.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Units, Markings and Behaviour of the Components in a Direct Current Circuit

pages.title: Units, Markings and Behaviour of the Components in a Direct Current Circuit
pages.body:
| **COMPONENT** | **UNIT OR MARKING** | **BEHAVIOUR IN A DIRECT CURRENT CIRCUIT** |
|---|---|---|
| **Capacitor** | Capacitance is measured in farads, written F. Most capacitors in school circuits are rated in microfarads. Some have a positive and a negative leg | When connected to a battery, current flows for a short time as the capacitor charges and then stops. The capacitor stores the charge. When it is connected across an LED it discharges, and the LED lights briefly and then fades |
| **Resistor** | Resistance is measured in ohms. Coloured bands on the resistor show its value | It limits the current. The larger the resistance, the smaller the current and the dimmer the LED. It works the same way whichever way round it is connected |
| **Diode** | It has two ends called the anode and the cathode. A band on the body marks the cathode | It allows current to pass in one direction only. It conducts when the anode is connected towards the positive terminal of the battery and blocks the current when it is reversed |
| **LED** | The longer leg is the anode and the shorter leg is the cathode | It gives out light only when it is connected the right way round. It must have a resistor in series to protect it from too large a current |

A simple way to study these components is to connect a battery, a switch, a resistor and an LED in series. The LED lights. Reverse the LED and it goes out. Replace the resistor with one of larger value and the LED becomes dimmer. Add a capacitor across the LED, charge it and then open the switch. The LED stays on for a moment as the capacitor discharges.

pages.title: Look at the picture
pages.body:
[[img:ib4ed90586|Fig 7.1  Charging and discharging of a capacitor in a DC circuit]]

Notice that during charging, current flows into the capacitor from the battery, building up stored charge, while during discharging, that same stored charge flows back out of the capacitor, powering the bulb briefly until the charge runs out. This charging and discharging behaviour is what allows capacitors to smooth out sudden changes in current or provide a short burst of stored energy when needed.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Capacitors are used in many everyday devices beyond simple demonstration circuits, including camera flash units, which store charge briefly before releasing it very quickly to create a bright flash, and computer memory, where tiny capacitors help store data temporarily. Understanding how capacitors charge and discharge in a simple DC circuit provides a foundation for understanding these more advanced, real world applications.
